title: Why Collections Could be Delegated Banking’s Toughest Challenge
summary: Could proactive debt collections help customers before payments are missed? Explore how banks can use technology, context and human support.
body_markdown:
*[Andrew Ducker](https://www.linkedin.com/in/andrew-ducker-28309a18/) asks what happens to delegated banking when the customer’s interests don’t match the bank’s.*


[Delegated banking](https://www.concentrix.com/from-digital-banking-to-delegated-banking/) sounds relatively straightforward when a bank is helping someone save more, avoid an unnecessary charge or prepare for a higher mortgage payment. It becomes rather more complicated when that customer owes the bank money.


Collections is where the promise of acting on a customer’s behalf faces its hardest test. The bank has a payment to recover. The customer may need to keep enough aside for food, energy bills and the next unexpected expense. The best answer for the bank today may not be the best one for the customer or even the bank next month.


So whose side is delegated banking on when those interests pull in different directions? And could a better collections journey begin before a payment is ever missed?


**Let’s start with a real-life scenario**


The customer of a bank hasn’t missed a mortgage payment. They’re not in arrears. As far as the bank’s collections team is concerned, there’s nothing to see.


But their fixed-rate deal ends in three months, and the new payment amount may be hard to find. The bank knows when the deal ends. The customer knows too, in theory. Understanding what the change means for their household budget is another matter.


So why does the most useful conversation so often begin *after* someone has missed a payment?


Waiting for customers to put up their hands will leave some people struggling in silence. Research in 2026[reported that 44% of people](https://www.stepchange.org/media-centre/press-releases/problem-debt-secret.aspx) who said they had experienced problem debt said they had told no one about it.


**Make the first message helpful**


Delegated banking could make a real difference here. A customer tells their bank what they want help with, and sets the parameters of what it’s allowed to do. That might include warning them about changes likely to squeeze their monthly budget.


How this is communicated will be key. An unsolicited message saying, “We think you’re going to struggle” could feel invasive. Whereas a message saying, “You asked us to flag changes that might affect your budget. Your mortgage payment could rise when your deal ends. Would you like to look at the options?” starts from a job the customer gave the bank.


They could compare mortgage options, see how a longer term affects the total they repay, or talk it through with someone. They might decide they’re fine. The point is to explain the implications while there’s time to act.


The permission needs to be clear too: what the bank will look for, what information it will use and how the customer can change their mind. Being invited to help is no excuse to watch everything.


FCA guidance addresses support[for mortgage customers who are worried about payments](https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/finalised-guidance/fg24-2-guidance-firms-supporting-existing-mortgage-borrowers-impacted-rising-living-costs?) as well as those already struggling. Delegation could help a bank offer it at precisely the moment that a customer has asked it to watch for.


**A warning isn’t the whole story**


A bank may know when a mortgage rate changes and see money coming in and going out of an account. With the right permissions, it might have a wider view of the customer’s finances.


That said, it would still have no idea that their partner has lost their job, that they’re supporting a parent, or that the apparent spare money in their account is already spoken for. Even a detailed credit record doesn’t explain what someone is living through.


Spotting a risk is one thing. Extrapolating from that to decide what someone can afford is another. The first may suit technology, but the latter calls for the customer’s input and, often, informed human judgement. The FCA’s expectations for firms supporting borrowers in difficulty include considering other debts, essential living costs and individual circumstances. A bank cannot – and should not – fill the gaps with assumptions.


An early warning should open a door by supplying some questions, ‘Does this look right to you?’ ‘Would it help to talk?’ It shouldn’t become an automated push towards the bank’s preferred repayment.


**What happens when the payment is missed?**


Early help isn’t going to be a panacea to fix every missed payment. Sometimes the explanation is straightforward: a payday has changed, a payment instruction hasn’t gone through or something has simply been forgotten. A clear digital route to sort that out may be exactly what the customer wants.


Technology might also make it easier to explore options privately before speaking to an adviser. Some people prefer to talk with a bot rather than a human, depending on the nature of what they’re sharing. Machines don’t make us feel judged (if we’ve programmed them correctly, at least).


A second missed payment may be a stronger signal that something persistent is going on, but it still doesn’t tell the bank why. The bank needs to recognise when it needs more context than a digital journey can safely establish.


**Make it easier to ask for help**


That handover deserves as much attention as the technology preceding it.[In the FCA’s Financial Lives 2024 survey](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/borrowers-financial-difficulty-project?) , among credit holders who had experienced, or were at risk of, payment difficulties but had not contacted their lender, 23% said they didn’t think the lender would be helpful. Another 21% felt too overwhelmed or stressed to deal with it.


If someone does begin to explain their situation, the bank should make that effort count. They shouldn’t have to repeat their story as they move from a digital assistant to servicing and then to collections. An adviser needs the context, a clear picture of the available options and enough authority to help agree a realistic next step. Where appropriate, that should include a route to free, independent debt advice.


There are real options to discuss and help can make a difference. Of the 1.7 million people who said they had used a debt advice or debt management service in the year to May 2024,[61% told the FCA](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/borrowers-financial-difficulty-project?) that their debts were more manageable as a result. Getting someone access to useful support is an outcome in its own right.


**Whose interests come first?**


As we’ve seen, collections poses some tough questions for a bank. It has money to recover, after all. The customer may need to protect enough money for food, energy bills and the next unexpected expense. Those interests won’t always point to the same immediate answer.


If an arrangement leaves nothing for essentials, a payment recovered today could become another missed payment next month. Acting on the customer’s behalf means taking that possibility seriously, even when the shorter-term numbers look good for the bank.


So the measure of a better collections journey can’t simply be whether the bank gets this month’s payment. It should also ask whether the customer understood their choices, whether the arrangement was affordable and whether they stayed out of difficulty afterwards.


Delegated banking won’t give a bank a complete account of someone’s life, or remove the need for a difficult conversation. It could, however, help start that conversation sooner, on the customer’s terms, with useful information already on the table. In collections, that may be the most valuable thing to delegate.
